mechanism: NSAIDs inhibit platelet function and can irritate the stomach lining; combined with an anticoagulant this raises bleeding risk, including serious GI bleeding.
management: Avoid combination when possible; if used, monitor closely for signs of bleeding.

mechanism: Additive antiplatelet and anticoagulant effects increase bleeding risk.
management: Use only with medical supervision.

mechanism: NSAID plus anticoagulant increases risk of serious bleeding.
management: Avoid combination when possible.

mechanism: Regular acetaminophen use (over ~2 g/day for several days) can increase INR and bleeding risk.
management: Occasional use is generally acceptable; monitor INR with regular use.

mechanism: Amiodarone inhibits warfarin metabolism, raising INR substantially.
management: Warfarin dose typically needs reduction; monitor INR closely.

mechanism: CYP2C9 inhibition increases warfarin exposure and INR.
management: Monitor INR closely.

mechanism: Thyroid hormone increases catabolism of clotting factors, enhancing warfarin effect.
management: Monitor INR when thyroid dose changes.

mechanism: Ibuprofen can interfere with aspirin's antiplatelet effect and adds GI bleeding risk.
management: Separate dosing timing if both are needed.

mechanism: NSAIDs can blunt the blood-pressure-lowering effect of ACE inhibitors and raise kidney strain, especially when dehydrated.
management: Use the lowest NSAID dose for the shortest time; stay hydrated.

mechanism: Two NSAIDs together add GI and kidney risk without extra benefit.
management: Do not combine.

mechanism: Corticosteroids plus NSAIDs increase risk of stomach ulcers and bleeding.
management: Consider stomach protection if both are needed.

mechanism: SSRIs reduce platelet serotonin; with NSAIDs the bleeding risk rises.
management: Watch for unusual bruising or bleeding.

mechanism: NSAIDs can reduce kidney function, which may affect metformin clearance in susceptible people.
management: Generally fine for short-term use in people with normal kidneys.

mechanism: ACE inhibitors raise potassium; adding potassium supplements can cause dangerously high levels.
management: Monitor potassium.

mechanism: Both raise potassium; combination risks hyperkalemia.
management: Monitor potassium and kidney function.

mechanism: ACE inhibitors may slightly enhance blood-sugar lowering.
management: Usually no change needed.

mechanism: NSAIDs can reduce the antihypertensive effect and raise kidney strain.
management: Use lowest NSAID dose for the shortest time.

mechanism: Corticosteroids raise blood sugar and can reduce metformin's effect.
management: Monitor blood sugar during steroid courses.

mechanism: Amiodarone raises atorvastatin levels, increasing muscle-injury risk.
management: Report unexplained muscle pain.

mechanism: CYP3A4 inhibition raises statin levels.
management: Short courses are usually tolerated; report muscle pain.

mechanism: Both increase serotonin; combination risks serotonin syndrome and seizures.
management: Avoid or use with close monitoring.

mechanism: SSRIs plus antiplatelets raise bleeding risk.
management: Watch for bruising or bleeding.

mechanism: Reduced stomach acid may lower levothyroxine absorption.
management: Take levothyroxine on an empty stomach; monitor thyroid labs.

mechanism: Calcium binds levothyroxine in the gut and reduces absorption.
management: Separate by at least 4 hours.

mechanism: Amlodipine raises simvastatin levels; muscle-injury risk rises at high statin doses.
management: Simvastatin dose is usually capped at 20 mg with amlodipine.

mechanism: Omeprazole inhibits CYP2C19, reducing clopidogrel activation and its protective effect.
management: A different acid reducer is often preferred.

mechanism: Different mechanisms; commonly used together short-term.
management: Keep each within its own daily maximum.
